nameStory: The lumpy bracket gets its name from the bumpy, irregular surface that develops as this fungus grows and ages. Unlike its smoother bracket fungi cousins, this species tends to form uneven, lumpy contours that make it look like someone crumpled up a piece of thick cardboard and stuck it to a tree.
description: The lumpy bracket is a shelf-like fungus that grows sideways out of dead hardwood trees and stumps, forming semicircular brackets. These tough, woody fungi are typically 3-6 inches across and have a distinctive bumpy upper surface that's usually gray or white when young. As they age, they often take on a greenish tint from algae growing on their surface, giving them a weathered, mossy appearance.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Semicircular shelf with distinctly lumpy, uneven surface texture that feels hard and woody; starts gray or white but often develops greenish patches from algae growth

idTips.label: Pores
idTips.description: Undersurface has elongated, maze-like pores rather than round ones; pores are white to cream colored and feel firm to the touch

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: No stem - grows directly from dead wood as a bracket or shelf

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Feels hard and woody like thick cardboard; old specimens may have small holes from beetle larvae boring into them

idTips.label: Safety
idTips.description: Not edible due to its tough, woody texture; never eat any wild mushroom without expert identification

habitat: Look for lumpy brackets on dead hardwood trees and old stumps, especially beech trees throughout New England's deciduous and mixed forests. They're commonly found in mature woodlands, along hiking trails, and in areas where trees have been cut or naturally fallen. These fungi prefer the dead wood of broadleaf trees rather than conifers.

seasonality.spring: Existing brackets from previous years are easily visible as trees leaf out. New growth may begin on fresh deadwood after spring rains.
seasonality.summer: Active growing season with fresh brackets developing their characteristic lumpy texture. Look for bright white edges on expanding specimens.
seasonality.fall: Peak visibility as leaves drop and expose brackets on trunks and branches. Older specimens show pronounced lumpy surfaces and possible algae greening.
seasonality.winter: Persistent year-round, these woody brackets remain attached and visible on bare trees, though growth slows significantly in cold weather.

funFact: Lumpy brackets are like apartment buildings for beetle larvae - the beetles actually prefer to lay their eggs in these fungi over the surrounding dead wood, creating a bustling insect neighborhood within the mushroom itself!
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other gray-white bracket fungi, but the distinctly lumpy, uneven surface texture sets it apart from smoother species. Memory trick: 'Lumpy by name, lumpy by nature' - if the surface isn't noticeably bumpy and irregular, it's probably not a lumpy bracket.
contextualKnowledge: The greenish coloration that develops on older specimens isn't part of the fungus itself but rather algae that grows on the surface, similar to how algae grows on tree bark or rocks in moist conditions.
compareHints: Unlike the smooth, velvety turkey-tail with its colorful concentric zones, lumpy bracket is much plainer and bumpier. The hairy bracket has a distinctly fuzzy surface texture, while lumpy bracket feels hard and woody. The elongated, maze-like pores also distinguish it from relatives with more circular pore patterns.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Turkey-tail differs from its Trametes relatives by having the most variable and vibrant color patterns - while Northern Cinnabar Polypore is distinctly reddish-orange and Hairy Bracket is notably fuzzy, turkey-tail displays the widest range of colors in distinct concentric bands.
Within the Trametes genus, this species stands out for its solid, brilliant orange color without the multicolored bands typical of Turkey-tail or the white/cream colors of many other relatives.
Among its Trametes relatives, Gilled Polypore is instantly distinguished by having true gills instead of the pores found in Turkey-tail or the maze-like patterns of White Maze Polypore.
Unlike its Trametes relatives like turkey-tail which form flat, colorfully zoned shelves, the little nest polypore is immediately recognizable by its unique cup shape.
Among its Trametes relatives, Hairy Bracket stands out for its distinctly fuzzy upper surface - most other species in this genus like Turkey-tail and Cinnabar Bracket have smooth, almost glossy caps.

Among the turkey-tail relatives, Trametes pubescens stands out for its uniform cream coloration and velvety texture, lacking the colorful zones of turkey-tail or the bright colors of cinnabar brackets.
